## Data and handling

- Input: Nasdaq TotalView-ITCH 5.0 sample `07302019.NASDAQ_ITCH50.gz` (30 July 2019), kept OUTSIDE the repository. Integrity: `gzip -t` passed and the size matched the expected 3,662,140,094 bytes (no checksum file was available). The terms of the sample are unclear, so it is treated as not redistributable: the repository contains only counts, summary statistics and tiny excerpts (the small JSON files in `bench/results/realdata/`).
- Guards: `.gitignore` patterns, `scripts/check_repo_size.py` (CI step and optional pre-commit hook `scripts/hooks/pre-commit`: fails on files over 2 MB or on archive/ITCH-looking names).
- CI never uses Nasdaq data: the `itch-synthetic` job runs the parser, validator, reference cross-check and replay benchmark on a synthetic ITCH file generated by our own code (`lob_itch synth`).
- Spec: Nasdaq NQTV-ITCH 5.0. Messages S, R, H, A, F, E, C, X, D, U, P, Q are decoded; other types are skipped by their length prefix. Skipped (unused) message types: I=3,723,793, J=2, L=210,706, V=1, Y=8,959.

### How the symbols for the reference-model comparison were chosen

All 8,849 symbols were validated for checks (a) and (b). The Stage 2 reference book (slow, O(n) per op) was run on SPY, AAPL, MSFT, TSLA, SCHP: SPY (busiest by message count), AAPL and MSFT (named liquid stocks), TSLA (execution-heavy, mid-ranked), and SCHP (the symbol whose message count equals the median over all symbols: the thinly traded case).

## Mapping ITCH to the engine

| ITCH | Engine operation |
|---|---|
| A / F | submit limit GTC (id = order reference, price in 1/10000 dollar = integer ticks). An add that would cross or lock our uncrossed book is counted and not inserted |
| D | cancel |
| X | partial cancel = `modify` down at the same price (keeps priority, the engine's modify rule); to zero = cancel |
| U | cancel + new order with the new reference (new queue position). Experiment `--replace-keeps-priority 1` keeps priority when the price is unchanged and the size does not increase |
| E / C | submit a marketable IOC on the opposite side at the executed order's price for the executed size; the ENGINE chooses the maker. Expected: exactly one trade against the executed reference at that price and size. C executions print at a different price from the order's, so the order's own price is used |
| P, Q | counted only (non-displayed and cross prints do not touch the displayed book) |
| S, H, Q(cross) | define the phase: before `S Q` pre-market, between `S Q` and `S M` market hours, after post-close. A symbol is in the continuous bucket when the phase is market hours, its trading state is `T`, it has had its opening cross and not its closing cross |

Why a pass of the priority check is meaningful: the IOC does not name the maker. If the engine's price-time rules, its modify rule or the replace handling differed from the exchange's for the book state built only from add/cancel/replace messages, the engine would hit a different order and the check fails; the unit tests contain such cases. A trivially echoing implementation could not fail; this one does, as the results show. After a disagreement the symbol's book is rebuilt from the exchange-implied state (arrival order) so one disagreement does not cascade.

Checks (all in `lob_itch validate`): (a) order-level consistency; (b) the engine-picks-the-maker priority check; (c) selected symbols also feed the Stage 2 reference book and BBO, every level aggregate and every queue order are compared every 5,000 per-symbol messages.

## Why does the exchange sometimes not follow strict FIFO? Hypotheses tested

The engine implements strict price-time priority and was NOT changed to make deviations disappear. Each hypothesis below is reported as supported, ruled out, partly tested or untestable from ITCH alone.

Experiment switches were run on the five reference symbols (SPY, AAPL, MSFT, TSLA, SCHP) over the full day, 153,389 continuous executions checked in each run:

| engine/mapping variant | deviations | change vs baseline |
|---|---|---|
| baseline mapping | 3,292 (2.15%) | - |
| replace (U) at the same price with size not increased keeps priority | 3,390 (2.21%) | +3.0% |
| partial cancel (X) loses priority | 3,550 (2.31%) | +7.8% |
| executions sharing a timestamp applied in queue order instead of feed order | 2,877 (1.88%) | -12.6% |

| # | hypothesis | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Self-match prevention (exchange skips a same-participant same-price order) | **untestable from ITCH** | executions do not name the aggressor; only F orders carry an MPID, and only 34 executed and 17 skipped orders among 115,364 deviations were F orders |
| 2 | Pegged / repriced orders re-ranked without a visible U | **partly untestable** | ITCH has no price-change message other than U (handled). 132,705 of 135,573 C executions print at a price different from the order's; E has no price field, so a silent reprice is not observable |
| 3 | Non-displayed / reserve interest causes the deviations | **not supported by the proxy** | per-symbol deviation rate vs non-displayed-activity proxy (shares in P trades per displayed executed share): Spearman -0.20; by quartile of the proxy the rate is 1.66%, 1.63%, 1.26%, 1.51%. A proxy, not a measurement: hidden interest that never prints is invisible |
| 4 | Odd-lot handling (odd lots lose priority to round lots) | **ruled out as the main cause** | in only 3,713 of 115,364 deviations (3.22%) were all orders ahead of the executed one odd lots by original size (4,006, 3.47%, by remaining size); the skipped order was an odd lot in 10.31%, the executed one in 8.68%; both round lot in 83.72%. Round-lot size per symbol taken from the R message. Minimum-quantity rules are untestable |
| 5 | Time structure (hour, time since open, last 5 minutes, ETP vs stock, price, burst gap, after halt) | **structure found, not an explanation** | rate is 2.75% for ETPs vs 1.41% for other symbols and falls with price (2.95% under $10 to 0.75% at $200 and over); see the tables below. Concentrated in a few symbols (top 10: 12.9% of deviations) |
| 6 | Same-timestamp messages out of matching order | **supported for a minority** | applying executions that share a timestamp in queue order removes 415 of 3,292 deviations (12.6%) on the five reference symbols; 3.51% of all deviations have the skipped order executed within 1 us. The feed's own sequence is what the engine replays |
| - | Replace keeps priority when price unchanged and size not increased | **ruled out** | 3,390 vs 3,292 deviations on the reference symbols |
| - | Partial cancel (X) loses priority | **ruled out** | 3,550 vs 3,292 deviations (more, not fewer) |
| - | Attributed (F) orders; orders created by replace | not explanatory | executed order created by replace in 8.48% of deviations, skipped in 11.83% (replaces are common in the feed in general) |
| - | Fate of the skipped order | descriptive | later cancelled or modified 35.72%, executed within 1 us 3.51%, within 1 ms 1.16%, later 14.03%, still resting at the end 0.00% |
| - | Gap between the two orders' adds | descriptive | within 1 us 0.03%, 1 ms 9.39%, 1 s 12.42%, over 1 s 78.15% (orders are mostly far apart in time, so this is not timestamp granularity) |

### Quantified attribution and unexplained remainder

- Same-timestamp execution ordering: removes 12.6% of deviations on the reference symbols (a measured effect of changing the replay order, not of changing the engine).
- Odd-lot de-prioritisation: at most 3.2% of deviations (all orders ahead odd lots), by original size; 3.5% by remaining size. This is an upper bound on what the hypothesis could explain, because the order ahead being odd is necessary, not sufficient.
- Even if the two effects were disjoint and fully additive, they would account for at most 15.8% of deviations; **at least 84.2% of the deviations are unexplained**.
- 115,363 of the 115,364 continuous deviations were a different order at the same price; 1 involved skipping a better-priced order; order-state violations: 0.
- Deviation rate by phase: pre-market 0.01%, continuous 1.51%, market hours outside the continuous window 0.41%, post-close 0.17%: deviations are concentrated in regular continuous trading.

### Interpretation

The engine's order-state tracking agrees with the exchange's exactly (0 violations over 278,286,223 messages), no execution ever skipped a better-priced order except 1 case(s), and in 98.5% of 7,631,594 continuous-hours executions strict price-time priority picked the very order the exchange executed. The remaining 1.5% are executions of a different order at the same price. Real exchanges apply rules beyond strict FIFO (display priority over non-displayed interest, reserve-order replenishment, self-trade prevention, special order types, odd-lot rules), none of which the feed exposes; this is the likely home of the residual but it is not demonstrated here. A small part comes from the order in which the feed lists executions that share a timestamp. Describe the result as: zero order-state violations, 1.5% of executions deviate from strict FIFO at the same price, a minority attributable to feed ordering, the rest unexplained from public data.

## Real-stream replay benchmark

Method: the ITCH stream is decoded once (decompression, parsing, bookkeeping and the engine, 201 s, NOT part of the measurement) while the exact operation stream applied to the engine for the selected symbols is recorded in memory; the timed replay then feeds that in-memory stream to fresh books (closed loop, single thread, in-memory pre-decoded op stream). 1 untimed warmup repetition and 7 measured repetitions; throughput from whole-loop wall time without per-op timers, latency from per-op TSC timestamps (rdtsc (lfence-serialised), timestamp pair overhead 40 ns, not subtracted). The event callback only counts events and trades.

Environment: AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX PRO 370 w/ Radeon 890M        (24 logical cores), Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0, flags `Release: /DWIN32 /D_WINDOWS /EHsc /O2 /Ob2 /DNDEBUG`, thread pinned to logical CPU 4 (efficiency class 1, see `bench/results/cpu_topology.txt`), CPU load measured before the run 24.2%. Desktop machine, not isolated; other workloads may run. CPU load measured before the run: 24.2% (limit for starting: 30.0%, attempt 3).

Workload: symbols AAPL, IWM, MSFT, MU, QQQ, SCHP, SPY, TQQQ, TSLA, URTY; 282,229,684 frames read; 64,369,644 engine operations over 10 books (add limit gtc: 57,582,152, cancel: 6,492,998, partial cancel modify: 35,326, execution marketable ioc: 253,870); 64,621,679 events, 257,333 trades; 0 orders resting at the end. Final book digests equal to the validation run's: 10 of 10 checked.

| metric | median | min | max | CV |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| throughput (Mops/s) | 2.46 | 2.27 | 2.59 | 4.0% |
| p50 latency (ns) | 160 | 150 | 160 | 2.9% |
| p99 latency (ns) | 2555 | 2435 | 2625 | 2.3% |
| p99.9 latency (ns) | 5040 | 4719 | 5190 | 2.9% |
| max latency (ns) | 15907300 | 2548230 | 82835900 | 109.1% |

|---|---|---|

Comparison with the synthetic Stage 3 workloads (same engine, same methodology, different pinned core class):

| workload | Mops/s | p50 ns | p99 ns | p99.9 ns |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| real ITCH replay | 2.46 | 160 | 2555 | 5040 |

| synthetic balanced | 9.32 | 130 | 381 | 771 |

Reading the comparison: the real stream is dominated by adds and deletes (executions are a few percent of operations), spread over several books whose depth and price dispersion differ from the synthetic generator's; a replace is two operations (cancel and add); resting books are deeper and more spread out than the synthetic ones, which touches more cache lines per operation. The benchmark is closed loop, single thread, over a pre-decoded stream for the chosen symbols only, on a desktop that was running other workloads: the CPU load before the run is recorded above and the run-to-run variance is shown; it says nothing about decoding throughput, multi-symbol contention or a live feed.

## Limitations

- One trading day (30 July 2019) of one venue's feed (Nasdaq); no other days, venues or years.
- ITCH 5.0 as of 2019: odd lots, order types and message sets have changed since.
- The matching rules being validated are our own strict price-time rules; the reference model is a second implementation by the same author, so the real data, not the reference model, is the independent check on the rules.
- ITCH shows displayed orders only: non-displayed and reserve quantity, participant identity and order types are invisible, which limits attribution of the FIFO deviations.
- Executions are validated one at a time against book state rebuilt from the exchange's own add/cancel/replace stream; after a deviation the book is resynchronised to the exchange state.
- Continuous-hours buckets are defined from system events, opening/closing crosses and trading-state messages; round-lot size comes from the directory message.
- The benchmark covers selected symbols over a pre-decoded stream and a closed loop on a non-isolated desktop.
